terms.meaning: A permanent member of a state who has civil and political rights and owes it loyalty.
A person ruled by someone else's state. Before 1947 Indians were British subjects.
A foreigner living in a state for a time, who is a citizen of another state.
Citizenship based on where a person is born.
Citizenship an alien gets after meeting set conditions.
One national citizenship only, with no separate state citizenship, as in India.
Citizenship of both the nation and the state, as in the USA.

items.name: Citizenship in ancient Greece
items.formula: Only those who took an active part in running the state.
items.example: Women, manual workers and slaves had no rights of citizenship.

items.name: Vattel's idea of a modern citizen
items.formula: A member of civil society, bound by duties and an equal receiver of its benefits.
items.example: The citizen is under the state's authority too.

items.name: Benefits a citizen enjoys
items.formula: Security, law and order, welfare schemes, fundamental rights, voting and contesting elections.
items.example: Only citizens can become President, Vice-President or a Supreme Court judge.

items.name: Citizen and alien compared
items.formula: Citizens: permanent, political rights, can't be driven out. Aliens: temporary, no political rights, can be asked to leave.
items.example: An expired visa or illegal activity can make an alien leave.

items.name: Domicile or residence
items.formula: Living long in a foreign state can earn citizenship.
items.example: England and USA: 5 years. France: 10 years.

items.name: Marriage
items.formula: A woman may get her foreign husband's citizenship, but usually not the reverse.
items.example: In Japan and some other countries the husband also gets it.

items.name: Service, application and property
items.formula: Government service abroad, applying with good character, or buying property.
items.example: Mexico has a rule on property.

items.name: The Citizenship Act
items.formula: Passed by Parliament in 1955, amended in 1986 and 2019.
items.example: Only Parliament can make citizenship law; state legislatures can't.

items.name: Citizenship by birth
items.formula: Born in India on or after 26 January 1950.
items.example: A child born in Mysuru in 2015 is a citizen by birth.

items.name: Citizenship by descent
items.formula: Born outside India on or after 26 January 1950, with a parent who was then an Indian citizen.

items.name: Citizenship by registration
items.formula: A non-citizen can become one by registering under the Constitution or the Act.
items.example: It is one of the 5 ways in India.

items.name: Citizenship by naturalization in India
items.formula: Foreigners apply to the President after living in India for at least 7 years.
items.example: Conditions must be met before applying.

items.name: Citizenship by incorporation of territory
items.formula: When a new territory joins India, its people get citizenship by government order.

items.name: Three ways to lose Indian citizenship
items.formula: Renunciation (by choice), Termination (taking another country's citizenship), Deprivation (fraud or disloyalty).
items.example: Deprivation is forced termination by the government.

items.name: Duties of a citizen
items.formula: Respect the Constitution, obey laws, pay taxes, oppose corruption and dowry, defend the nation.
items.example: Rights and duties are two faces of the same coin.

items.name: Fundamental duties in our Constitution
items.formula: Added in 1976 by the 42nd Amendment, under Article 51A.
items.example: They remind citizens of their social and economic obligations.

mistakes.text: Renunciation is done by the citizen's own choice. Termination happens by law when another citizenship is taken.
India has single citizenship. Living in Karnataka doesn't give a separate Karnataka citizenship.
India's naturalisation period is 7 years. The 5 and 10 years are England or USA and France.
